result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.greedy_color()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Color the graph using a greedy algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L26536-L26645){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.greedy_color( strategy="largest_first", interchange=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Greedy coloring](/assets/graphs/greedy-color.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A strip of four triangles on six nodes, each node filled with the color of its class: C and F in the accent color, A and D in teal, B and E in violet. No edge joins two nodes of the same color, and the card lists the three classes 0, 1, 2." width="100%"} Graph coloring assigns colors (represented as integers) to nodes such that no two adjacent nodes share the same color. The greedy algorithm processes nodes in a specified order and assigns the smallest available color to each node. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [strategy]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["largest_first"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The strategy for ordering nodes during coloring. Options are: `"largest_first"` (the default), `"smallest_last"`, `"saturation_largest_first"`, `"independent_set"`, `"random"`, and `"arbitrary"`. See the *Strategy Types* section for more information. [interchange]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use color interchange optimization (not yet implemented). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary mapping node IDs to their assigned color (0-indexed integers). The colors are consecutive integers starting from 0. ::: ## Strategy Types {.doc-strategy-types} There are several strategies that can be used: - `"largest_first"`: process high-degree nodes first; often produces good results by handling constrained nodes early - `"smallest_last"`: Process nodes in reverse order of removal by minimum degree; often produces optimal or near-optimal colorings - `"saturation_largest_first"` or `"dsatur"`: DSATUR algorithm that prioritizes nodes with the most differently-colored neighbors; often produces excellent results - `"independent_set"`: colors independent sets iteratively - `"random"`: random node ordering - `"arbitrary"`: process in the order nodes appear in the graph ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Greedy coloring is what every graph-coloring course starts with and what most real software uses in practice, despite its worst-case wastefulness. Its output size is bounded above by $\Delta(G) + 1$, where $\Delta$ is the maximum degree (a Brooks-style bound), and by exactly $2$ on bipartite graphs. The `strategy=` argument controls the crucial ordering step. *DSATUR* (Brélaz, 1979) is the strongest general-purpose default: it colors the highest-saturation node next, meaning the node whose neighborhood already uses the most distinct colors, and consistently produces optimal or near-optimal colorings for typical graphs. *smallest_last* peels the minimum-degree node last and applies its coloring in reverse peeling order, matching DSATUR on many sparse inputs; *largest_first* is faster but coarser. Because the underlying problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, none of these strategies guarantees the true chromatic number, but running several and taking the best is a cheap and effective heuristic. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A 4-cycle is bipartite, so a greedy coloring only needs 2 colors, alternating around the square: ::: {#4ef00a7f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "D") .add_edge("D", "A") ) coloring = graph.greedy_color() # Returns e.g., {1: 0, 2: 1, 3: 0, 4: 1} (2 colors for a square) coloring ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {3: 0, 1: 0, 4: 1, 2: 1} ``` ::: ::: A triangle is a different story: since every node is adjacent to both others, no two can share a color, so 3 colors are required no matter which strategy is used: ::: {#0f42bb7a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "A") ) coloring = graph.greedy_color(strategy="dsatur") num_colors = len(set(coloring.values())) # Returns 3 (colors for a triangle) num_colors ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
